name: Self-defeating prophecy
statement: A published prediction can prevent what it predicts, because the people who hear it change what they do, and the forecast is then read as an error.
meaning: Merton's self-fulfilling prophecy, entry 44, has a twin that he named and then put aside. A prediction is made public, people act on it, and their actions push the world away from the state it described. Two conditions have to hold. The prediction must reach the people whose behaviour matters, and their response must run against it rather than with it. Neither is automatic. The same publicity that can make a forecast self-defeating can make it self-fulfilling, which is what the bandwagon effect describes, so the direction is a question for measurement rather than for definition. A conditional projection is a separate case. A model saying an epidemic reaches a given size if nothing is done has not predicted that size, it has stated what inaction would cost, and its non-occurrence after action is the model working. The idea is also distinct from the preparedness paradox, entry 142, which is about how averted harm gets judged afterwards rather than about a prediction undoing itself. The twin is the harder of the two to evidence. A prediction that prevents itself leaves no clean counterfactual, so the outcome that did not arrive has to be modelled rather than observed.

origin.where: The Antioch Review, volume 8, issue 2, pages 193-210
origin.note: The idea appears in one footnote of the paper that made its twin famous. It reads: 'Counterpart of the self-fulfilling prophecy is the "suicidal prophecy" which so alters human behavior from what would have been its course had the prophecy not been made, that it fails to be borne out. The prophecy destroys itself.' Merton adds that this important type is not considered here. He refers the reader to R. M. MacIver's The More Perfect Union, published by Macmillan in 1948, for examples of both types, and to his own 1936 paper in the American Sociological Review for a general statement. His name for it was 'suicidal prophecy'. Where the phrase 'self-defeating prophecy' first appeared in print could not be established. The earliest title carrying it that a Crossref title search returns is Bernard Grofman's 1974 chapter 'Rational Choice Models and Self-Fulfilling and Self-Defeating Prophecies', which uses the plural; the earliest carrying the singular phrase is from 2014. A Crossref title search on 'suicidal prophecy' returns nothing, and the Google Books API refused both attempts on 21 September 2026 with a rate limit.

evidence: The formal treatment came six years after Merton and is a proof rather than a measurement. Simon asked under what conditions a public prediction that influences behaviour is still confirmed. He defines a bandwagon effect as people being more likely to vote for a candidate when they expect him to win, and an underdog effect as the reverse. Writing the actual vote as a function of the published prediction, he shows that a prediction which is borne out always exists provided that function is continuous, by Brouwer's fixed-point theorem. He credits Grunberg and Modigliani with solving the problem for certain cases of economic prediction. The empirical work sits in elections. Sudman reviewed the exit-poll studies and concluded that exit polls appear to cause small declines in total voting in areas where the polls close late for those elections where the exit polls predict a clear winner when previously the race had been considered close. That sentence was read from his abstract at an earlier check, and the abstract could not be reopened on 21 September 2026. Morton, Muller, Page and Torgler used a French voting reform under which some overseas territories voted after mainland exit poll results were public. The published abstract reports that knowing the exit poll information decreases voter turnout by about 11 percentage points, and that it increases bandwagon voting, so those who do turn out are likelier to vote for the expected winner. Westwood, Messing and Lelkes ran two studies on probabilistic forecasts. In the first, 4,151 respondents from wave 25 of Pew's American Trends Panel saw a hypothetical Senate projection given either as a vote share or as a win probability. Those shown the probability were on average 7% more certain about who would win. Shown an 87% chance of victory, participants expected the candidate to take 64.6% of the vote, 95% CI 63.0% to 66.2%; shown the equivalent 55% vote share, they expected 56.5%, 95% CI 55.3% to 57.6%. Thirty-eight per cent gave the same number for expected vote share and likelihood of victory. In the second, 1,171 respondents took 5,845 trials of a five-round game in which voting cost $1 and the round's result won or lost $2. Voting fell as the stated probability moved away from even odds, b = -0.17, p = 4.2 x 10-5. An advantage of 20% over even odds lowered voting by 3.4%, 95% CI 1.8% to 5.1%, and an advantage of 40% lowered it by 6.9%, 95% CI 3.6% to 10.2%. Vote share extremity had no detectable effect, b = -0.13, p = .48. The epidemic case is a single episode rather than a study. Meltzer and colleagues projected in September 2014 that Liberia and Sierra Leone would have about 550,000 Ebola cases, 1.4 million corrected for underreporting, by 20 January 2015, extrapolating trends without additional interventions or changes in community behaviour. The CDC's 2016 retrospective states that although initial model estimates of Ebola represented a worst-case scenario, the international community responded to ensure that these dire predictions would not be realised. Record and Pershing put the mechanism inside an epidemic model, letting the contact rate respond to the forecast. In their simulations a faster response by the population to the system or to a forecast lowers the peak of infections, and responding to a forecast lowers that peak further than responding to current infection levels. They are modelling the feedback rather than observing it, and they say so.

replication.headline: Conclusive forecasts do cut turnout, by about 11 percentage points in the cleanest field test. Whose turnout they cut is disputed, and two studies find the leader's side turning out more.
replication.detail: The mechanism and the direction come apart. That a published forecast of a decisive outcome lowers participation is found by three designs: Sudman's review of exit polls, Morton and colleagues' natural experiment at about 11 percentage points, and Westwood, Messing and Lelkes's incentivised game at 3.4% for an advantage of 20% over even odds and 6.9% for an advantage of 40%. The self-defeating part of the claim is that this falls on the predicted winner's supporters, and that is where the studies disagree. Morton and colleagues report that exit poll information increases bandwagon voting, which runs with the forecast rather than against it. Agranov, Goeree, Romero and Yariv, in laboratory elections, report that voting propensity increases systematically with subjects' predictions of their preferred alternative's advantage, that polls lead to more participation by the expected majority, and that they generate more landslide elections. Their 2016 discussion paper, read in full and carrying that abstract word for word, ran 22 groups of nine subjects through 440 elections. In it, voting propensity was 0.29 where the laboratory poll suggested a substantial loss for the subject's preferred alternative and 0.60 where it suggested a toss-up, a difference they report at the 1% level. Where the poll suggested a landslide victory the rate was 0.49, which they report as not distinguishable from the toss-up rate. Those three figures come from the discussion paper and could not be checked against the published article. Westwood and colleagues report no evidence of directional differences in their game, citing their appendix table A16, so the demobilisation they measure is not confined to the leading side. Their survey experiment does find the certainty effect stronger when the candidate was ahead in the polls. Two of their smaller replications, on Amazon Mechanical Turk with 275 participants and on a Qualtrics panel with 178, recovered the same perceptual pattern across offices and when the rival candidate was the one ahead.

study.cite: Westwood, S. J., Messing, S., & Lelkes, Y. (2020). Projecting Confidence: How the Probabilistic Horse Race Confuses and Demobilizes the Public. The Journal of Politics, 82(4), 1530-1544.

limits: Nothing found here tests the general claim. Every quantitative result is about elections, and within elections about turnout rather than about a forecast being falsified. Record and Pershing, who model the feedback rather than observe it, write that it is not clear whether a reflexive forecast could ever be verified empirically. Westwood and colleagues measure a paid game and an online panel, not votes cast; they say so, and call for field replication. Around 93% of their survey respondents reported an intent to vote in all conditions, and they treat that turnout result as exploratory. The Morton figure has two versions. The published abstract, read at EconPapers, gives about 11 percentage points. The preprint of 5 February 2013 in Queensland University of Technology's repository, read in full here, gives about 12, and reports a preferred specification of almost 12 percentage points with a robust standard error of 1.7. Westwood and colleagues cite the published article for a full 12 percentage point decrease, which is the preprint's number. The published article itself was not opened: ScienceDirect answered with a Cloudflare block rather than a paywall, and Unpaywall records no open copy. Sudman's abstract was read at the previous check and could not be reopened on 21 September 2026, Oxford Academic serving a Cloudflare challenge, PsycNET blocking the record, and neither Crossref nor Semantic Scholar carrying the abstract. Agranov and colleagues' published article was not opened either. Oxford Academic returns 403, the Zurich repository copy that Unpaywall lists as open sits behind an Anubis proof-of-work challenge, and the CaltechAUTHORS record holds only a zip of supplementary files. Their 2016 discussion paper for the Wissenschaftszentrum Berlin is open and is the source for the laboratory figures above. Delli Carpini's 1984 study of the networks' early call of the 1980 race is named across this literature, by Westwood and colleagues among others. JSTOR serves a bot challenge for it, Unpaywall records no open copy, and no figure from it appears above. Merton's 1936 paper was not opened in English, JSTOR again answering with a bot challenge, so nothing is claimed about what it says, only that his 1948 footnote points to it. A complete Russian translation, published in Sotsiologichesky Zhurnal in 2009 and indexed at DOAJ, is open, and was read only far enough to confirm that it is a translation of the 1936 article. MacIver's 1948 book is held at the Internet Archive in two scans, both restricted to lending, and was not read. Grunberg and Modigliani's paper is closed at the University of Chicago Press, which serves a bot challenge. The epidemic material is one projection and one retrospective by an overlapping set of authors at the same agency, which is a source with an interest in the answer. Searching on 21 September 2026 covered Crossref by title, Unpaywall, Semantic Scholar, Europe PMC, DOAJ, the Internet Archive, EconPapers, EconStor, cdc.gov and general web search. The Google Books API refused both attempts with a rate limit, and EconStor returned 503.
misreadings: The name is not Merton's and the idea is not his subject. He called it a suicidal prophecy, gave it four sentences in a footnote, and wrote that it is not considered here. Treating the entry as the second half of his 1948 argument overstates what that paper contains. The second error is to read a conditional projection as a prophecy. Meltzer and colleagues reached 1.4 million cases by extrapolating trends without additional interventions or changes in community behaviour, so the figure is what inaction was estimated to cost. A projection stated that way cannot be falsified by a response that follows it. The third is the direction. The version that circulates is that forecasts of a comfortable win demobilise the winner's supporters and hand the election to the underdog, and the studies do not deliver that. Morton and colleagues find bandwagon voting rising, Agranov and colleagues find the expected majority participating more, and Westwood and colleagues find no directional difference in the behaviour they measure. What survives is that conclusive information about an outcome lowers turnout on both sides. The fourth is the impossibility argument, that reflexivity makes social prediction futile. Simon's answer is that a confirmed prediction always exists where the reaction function is continuous, and that his proof refutes allegations commonly made about the impossibility, in principle, of correct prediction of social behaviour. His practical caveat is narrower and sharper: the forecaster would have to know the reaction function, and it is less obvious where that knowledge comes from. Naming a case is not testing one. Tenenboim-Weinblatt's chapter on the 2016 election carries the term in its title. The MIT Press Reader extract of it, read at the previous check, sets out scenarios rather than measurements, and that page returned 403 on 21 September 2026.
